body_en:
## Fourth quarter: Shanahan and his quarterbacks

## Shanahan's QB history

First, an overview of every quarterback who started a regular-season game with Kyle Shanahan as the play-caller:

| From | To | Player | Team |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2008 | 2009 | Matt Schaub | Texans |
| 2008 | | Sage Rosenfels | Texans |
| 2010 | | Donovan McNabb | Redskins |
| 2010 | 2011 | Rex Grossman | Redskins |
| 2011 | | John Beck | Redskins |
| 2012 | 2013 | Robert Griffin III | Redskins |
| 2012 | 2013 | Kirk Cousins | Redskins |
| 2014 | | Brian Hoyer | Browns |
| 2014 | | Connor Shaw | Browns |
| 2014 | | Johnny Manziel | Browns |
| 2015 | 2016 | Matt Ryan | Falcons |
| 2017 | | Brian Hoyer | 49ers |
| 2017 | 2020 | C.J. Beathard | 49ers |
| 2017 | 2022 | Jimmy Garoppolo | 49ers |
| 2018 | 2020 | Nick Mullens | 49ers |
| 2021 | 2022 | Trey Lance | 49ers |
| 2022 | 2024 | Brock Purdy | 49ers |
| 2023 | | Sam Darnold | 49ers |
| 2024 | | Brandon Allen | 49ers |
| 2024 | | Joshua Dobbs | 49ers |

Over more than 17 years, Kyle Shanahan has sent 20 quarterbacks onto the field who then received his instructions through the radio in their helmets. And despite this turnover, he managed to field strong offenses almost everywhere, for example:

- Matt Schaub: passing leader in 2008
- Robert Griffin III: Rookie of the Year in 2012
- Matt Ryan: MVP in 2016
- Jimmy Garoppolo: 6 wins in his first 6 games in 2017
- Nick Mullens: third quarterback in NFL history with the most passing yards through his first 13 starts ([post by @RufusRufus615, December 8, 2020](https://twitter.com/RufusRufus615/status/1336147074778341377))
- Brock Purdy: San Francisco 49ers single-season passing record in 2023

So the question is: how does Shanahan manage to make these players, who apart from rookie RGIII and Matt Ryan mostly came from the second tier, look so good and still put such a productive offense on the field? This very question keeps sparking debates within the American football bubble. And often it leads to the quarterback's performance being downplayed:

> "…Shanahan + scheme + weapons prevent that better than anyone, by a mile. No other QB gets anywhere near as many 'easy' looks in the passing game, i.e. base personnel, single-high defenses, clear matchups and clear space, little complexity." (translated from German)
>
> Adrian Franke (@adrianbb89), [January 2, 2024](https://twitter.com/adrianbb89/status/1742172227536125991)

## Specific demands on the quarterback

The previous parts already explained in detail how Shanahan builds his playbook, puts together the game plan and calls his plays, but what exactly does he want to see from the quarterback? First of all, it should be said that in their general approach, many other top offensive coaches won't act very differently. They scout intensively, find weak spots and try to bring out their strengths as well as possible. What probably makes the difference, though, is that only a few coaches plan their plays so meticulously down to the last detail and thereby give the players, especially the QB, a concrete plan to act on. Other coaches may rely more on football intelligence (McDaniels with Brady, Payton with Brees) or on improvisational skills and athleticism (Reid with Mahomes, McDermott/Brady with Allen), but for Shanahan that is not the priority. Rather, he believes that his plays have the answer built in for almost every conceivable scenario, and the QB only has to identify the scenario correctly and then act according to the given scheme.

In Michael Silver's book, the phrase "**plays over players**" keeps coming up. It describes a philosophy in which the design of a play is considered more important than the individual abilities of a single player. This means that the success of a play does not depend on an exceptional athlete making an outstanding individual effort, but on whether the scheme is so well thought out that it works regardless of individual talent, as long as everyone sticks to the plan. As a result, the QB carries much less responsibility than in other offenses, for example. He usually doesn't have to adjust the protection (in Shanahan's system the center does that) or actively send receivers onto different routes. The only adjustment left to the QB is that the play-caller usually gives him a second play as well. He can switch to it before the snap if he thinks the defense is well set up against the original call. This is called the "CAN" call. Often it is a run when a pass was originally called, or vice versa. This simplification really does make it easy for the QB to find his way in the offense and thus gives the offense a high floor, but it can also hold back the offense, or the players' individual class, if they are only allowed to "work to rule." Tensions can arise especially with QBs who were already successful in more complex offenses.

While Kyle Shanahan was offensive coordinator of the Atlanta Falcons (2015–2016), there were tensions with quarterback Matt Ryan. These differences were largely due to Shanahan's "plays over players" approach.

Shanahan demanded that Ryan stick strictly to the given reads and not rely on individual creativity. Ryan, an experienced quarterback, was used to having more freedom at the start of a play, which was severely restricted under Shanahan. At the beginning of Shanahan's time with the Falcons in 2015, Ryan struggled to execute the system exactly the way Shanahan demanded, which led to a below-average season.

In the 2016 season, the two agreed on compromises: Shanahan gave Ryan more control at the line of scrimmage, while Ryan subordinated himself more to the system. According to Michael Silver's account, a fair amount of tequila is said to have flowed when Shanahan, Ryan and QB coach Matt LaFleur hashed out this agreement during a vacation in Cabo, Mexico.

As a result, the Falcons had a historically strong offense in the 2016 season and reached Super Bowl LI. Ryan won the NFL MVP award with his best statistical season. The combination of Shanahan's structure and Ryan's abilities produced an almost perfect offensive machine.

According to numerous executives and scouts, there are 10 to 16 key attributes, depending on the scouting model, by which a QB is evaluated. Even if in theory everyone arrives at the same individual grades, coaches will ultimately prefer different players, because their respective systems have different requirements. So for Shanahan, the requirements for the QB are not necessarily a particularly strong arm or agile, fast legs (more of a nice-to-have); for him, the QB has to have quick comprehension, decisiveness and the ability to anticipate.

The cautionary example here is Trey Lance, for whom the team paid a high price but who never developed as hoped. In particular, he lacked the ability to read the field quickly, draw the right conclusions and then distribute the ball in rhythm. He did have a strong arm and supposedly fast legs, though at the NFL level that never looked anything like it did in college, but he was often too hesitant, held the ball too long or didn't focus on his technique, so his passes became inaccurate. On top of that came unfortunate injuries, so he never got the experience to make up for his deficits. Shanahan therefore abandoned the project quickly and could count himself lucky to have found in Purdy a seventh-round QB who could execute the system exactly the way Shanahan wanted. On top of that, Purdy could even offer improvisational skills that no QB in the Shanahan scheme had shown before, with the exception of Matt Ryan.

The key factors for Shanahan are therefore:

- The QB has to move through Shanahan's progression-based system quickly, i.e. be able to scan the field and the defense fast.
- A "hitch-and-throw" mentality: no long hesitation in the pocket.
- Deep throws are generally less important than accurate passes over the middle.
- "Anticipation throws": throwing into windows before the receiver gets there.

## Shanahan's idiosyncratic analyses

When it comes to analyzing the game, though, Shanahan often has his own opinion, which can differ sharply from those of analysts, former players or podcasters. Especially since he drew up the game plan, he knows what he asked of the QB and how the QB was supposed to behave in certain situations. This can go one way, where the QB delivered a successful play but Shanahan is still angry with him because he didn't stick to the plan, or the other way, where Shanahan says the QB did everything right because he played it exactly as discussed in the QB room before the game. The 2015 season with Matt Ryan in particular can serve as an example, when conflicts between Ryan and Shanahan became more frequent. There have also been scenes with Brock Purdy where Shanahan didn't like Purdy breaking away from the play call like that.

On the other hand, there are also scenes that did not end well but in which, contrary to public opinion, Shanahan did not blame his QB because he behaved exactly as discussed before the game. An example is the following interception in the game against the Rams in December 2024:

> "…he has to hit the throw to Pearsall just before that in that moment, or at least give Pearsall a chance. He had already missed him downfield against Chicago. The INT itself: the checkdown was wide open for 5+ yards on 2nd down. The shot was never there." (translated from German)
>
> Adrian Franke (@adrianbb89), [December 13, 2024](https://twitter.com/adrianbb89/status/1867505537409228829)

As the post shows, podcaster and TV analyst Adrian Franke was quickly certain that Purdy had made a massive mistake here by throwing deep to Jauan Jennings, who was running deep after a double move, instead of taking the easy throw to the open receiver underneath. On the face of it, the outcome proves him right.

Early on, however, there were also other opinions holding that the receiver bore at least part of the blame (or even the officials), because he broke off the route too early and at the very least should have prevented the interception. Here is the clip from JT O'Sullivan's analysis on QB School:

> "A former player sees it more like Manuel…" (translated from German)
>
> Chris Pracher (@CPracher497), [December 14, 2024](https://twitter.com/CPracher497/status/1867878325936660483)

And indeed, after the game Kyle Shanahan confirmed that Purdy had basically made the right decision here, since it was exactly the look the team had hoped for on this play before the game: the WR one-on-one against the smaller CB, who was expected to bite on the stutter step, after which Jennings should win the matchup. Unfortunately, that's not how it went, and Shanahan also blamed, among other things, the early pressure from the defensive line and a missing flag from the officials, but he saw no mistake in Purdy's read.

> Kyle Shanahan says the Rams should have been flagged for illegal contact on Brock Purdy's interception
>
> Coach Yac (@Coach_Yac), [December 18, 2024](https://twitter.com/Coach_Yac/status/1869488735001456758)

And this shows quite well the dangers that lie even in the otherwise much-praised Shanahan scheme, when a play should work based on the scouting results but outside circumstances, such as officiating decisions, receiver mistakes or unexpected defensive calls like the blitz by Chiefs CB Trent McDuffie in the 2024 Super Bowl, mean that it doesn't. There is still potential here for Shanahan to develop his scheme further. Perhaps together with a smart QB who can be given more responsibility, as Matt Ryan was in 2016.

## Are all Shanahan QBs "game managers"?

At least since the Jimmy Garoppolo era, the myth has persisted that basically any QB could look good and play successfully in Shanahan's offense. But anyone who looks at the list of QBs who have started under Kyle Shanahan will quickly see that this is not the case. As described, the QB also needs certain key attributes to exploit the system perfectly.

Quarterbacks who play in Kyle Shanahan's system are often called "game managers," a description suggesting that their main job is to execute the play-calling efficiently rather than to decide games through individual brilliance. But does that automatically mean quarterbacks under Shanahan are weaker than their colleagues in other systems? The answer is more complex than it seems at first glance. In fact, Shanahan has proven several times that he can lift quarterbacks who were considered mediocre outside his system to a higher level of performance, even if they are rarely perceived as true elite playmakers.

A look at recent NFL history shows that quarterbacks such as Jimmy Garoppolo, Jared Goff or Ryan Tannehill played consistently productive football in systems from the Shanahan school, but without performing at an MVP level individually. Garoppolo led the 49ers to the Super Bowl in 2019, but in classic dropback situations without play-action he was only the 19th-best passer in the league. Jared Goff also reached the Super Bowl with the Rams under Sean McVay but was never considered an outstanding individual quarterback. Tannehill, who had little success in Miami, saw a noticeable improvement in Tennessee under a related scheme. All these examples show that the Shanahan system tends to make average quarterbacks more productive in a structured environment, without them being considered top QBs in the league as a result.

The reason lies in the way Shanahan's offense is built. His system is based on clearly structured progression reads, play-action, motion and defined passing windows that make it easier for the quarterback to distribute the ball quickly and efficiently. This reduces the quarterback's individual influence, since many throws are created by the scheme and not by exceptional athletic talent. Shanahan's offense does not demand deep, risky passes into tight windows but relies on precision in the short and intermediate game and on yards after the catch (YAC) generated by the playmakers. At the same time, Shanahan's quarterbacks are expected to stick strictly to the progression and not deviate from the structure. This "plays over players" philosophy makes the scheme more important than the playmaker's individual class.

However, that does not mean quarterbacks under Shanahan are automatically limited. The best counterexample is Matt Ryan, who played an MVP season in Shanahan's offense in 2016 and led the Falcons to the Super Bowl. A year earlier, Ryan had still struggled to execute the system exactly, and the next year he was the league MVP. Brock Purdy, too, shows that a quarterback with the right traits, namely quick processing, accurate short passes and disciplined play execution, can be exceptionally successful under Shanahan, and with his agility and improvisational skills he brings a new level to the offense that Shanahan has not had before.

Above all, it is difficult to compare players who play in different systems that place different demands on the QB. If a QB is not used according to his strengths, he will not be successful there either, even if he may rank among the top 3 at his position in certain attributes. The best coaches are distinguished by making the most of their QBs' strengths and avoiding situations in which their weaknesses stand out. You could never have put Peyton Manning in an option offense, or Drew Brees in an Air Raid offense with lots of deep balls. And it is the same with Kyle Shanahan's quarterbacks, the "game managers." The system generally does not require them to hold the ball for a long time and then throw 30 yards deep to the X receiver's back shoulder while falling backward. Instead, it takes quick recognition of the game situation and good decisions. In line with the motto "to each their own," one can say that even though the position has the same name and the basic task is identical, a direct comparison between QBs in different systems and teams has only limited meaning, if any.

## Overtime

## Criticism

Of course, an article like this should also mention critical voices. In his book, Michael Silver writes above all that Shanahan as a coach finds it hard to shine in so-called soft skills. He can be very direct and even unfriendly toward his assistants and players, which some former assistants complained about after their time under Shanahan. That is said to be one of the main differences between him and McVay, who seems to come across as much more charming and understanding. Assistants such as Mike McDaniel or Matt LaFleur also report that they, like players such as Matt Ryan or Jimmy Garoppolo, frequently clashed loudly with Shanahan. This probably reveals a slightly choleric streak in Shanahan, of the kind you also know from fine dining, for example, where perfection matters just as much as in Shanahan's system.

Shanahan has also been criticized in the past for his play-calling in big games. His decisions in Super Bowl LI (as the Falcons' offensive coordinator) and Super Bowl LVIII (as the 49ers' head coach) in particular are up for debate, as in both he failed to close out a clear lead. Another weakness of Shanahan's is his tendency to cling too tightly to his system even when defenses adjust to it. In recent years, many teams have started to use two-high-safety defenses to defuse Shanahan's play-action passing game. Only in 2024 did Shanahan begin to shift his system more toward classic dropback passing, and then he almost overdid it, because without screens and with little play-action he didn't make things easy for the QB.

## Conclusion

Kyle Shanahan created his system from the many years of experience of his mentors Mike Shanahan, Jon Gruden and Gary Kubiak and turned it into one of the most copied and adapted systems in the entire NFL. Even though Sean McVay's sister system is probably the trendier version by now and his assistant coaches are in greater demand, practically every coach says that Kyle Shanahan is still the original and that learning from him was a fundamental experience for everyone. Especially because the scheme manages to lift even average QBs to a competitive level, it now serves across the league as a template for many young coaches who don't get to work with one of the four or five elite QBs. It will be interesting to see what the next stages of the system's evolution look like, especially as Shanahan develops even more trust in QB Brock Purdy, who has now signed an expensive contract, which meant previous key players such as Deebo Samuel had to be let go.

**The spark for this article was reading Michael Silver's book, which really offers a very deep look at the inner workings of an NFL coaching staff.**

**I hope every reader can take something from this article to be prepared for future discussions whenever it's all about the "scheme" again.**

Go Niners!
